title: Krishna Counsels Arjuna to Abduct Subhadra
story:
The festival on Raivataka had everything a festival should have, and more of it than anyone could take in at once.

The Vrishnis and the Andhakas had gathered on the mountain to make merry, and they threw themselves into it completely. Musicians struck up and dancers danced and singers sang, and the young men of the Vrishni race, brilliant with ornaments, rode about in cars decked with gold. Mansions set with gems and artificial trees of bright color rose around the hill, and citizens came by the hundreds and thousands, some on foot and some in fine chariots, with their wives and their followers. Balarama roved at will, cheerful with drink, with Revati beside him and musicians trailing after. Pradyumna and Samba, ever eager for battle, roamed the ground flushed and garlanded with bright flowers, disporting themselves like a pair of celestials. King Ugrasena moved through it all with his thousand wives, and Akrura and Sarana and Gada and Satyaki and Uddhava and a hundred other heroes, each with his own train, adorned the mountain. It was a festival loud enough to forget yourself in. Both clans had turned out for it, and no one thought of anything but the day.

Through all of it two friends walked together, seeing everything: Krishna and Arjuna, who was there in his wandering years, far from his brothers, and whom Krishna had made welcome. And as they wandered, they came upon a young woman in the midst of her maids — Subhadra, the daughter of Vasudeva, Krishna's own sister, decked with every ornament and lovely to look upon.

Arjuna stopped. The great archer, the man who had ranged the wilds and faced a hundred dangers without flinching, stood still as a struck bell. The battle-hardened warrior, who had never once flinched at an enemy, could not look away. The god of desire had taken him, and it showed all over his face. The drums and the singing went on around them, but Arjuna no longer heard them; the whole bright festival had narrowed to a single figure.

Krishna noticed at once, because Krishna noticed everything. He looked at his friend — this tiger among men, suddenly struck dumb — and smiled.

'How is this?' he asked. 'Can the heart of one who ranges the woods be agitated by the god of desire?' It was the smile more than the words that undid Arjuna. 'This is my sister, Partha, the sister of Sarana and the favourite daughter of my father. Tell me if your heart is fixed upon her, and I shall speak to my father myself.'

Arjuna answered as a man in his condition must, and his answer was honest. She was Vasudeva's daughter and Krishna's sister, he said, and with so much beauty, whom could she not fascinate? What heart would not be stirred?

And so, warm and unhurried, Krishna turned matchmaker. Rather than leave the matter to the slow formality of self-choice, he counseled Arjuna to carry Subhadra away by force — the celebrated Kshatriya form of marriage. It was counsel given with a smile, between friends, and it set in motion everything that followed. There was nothing solemn about it; Krishna made the matter sound as simple as it was bold. The seed of the plan was planted there in the noise of the festival, and it would not take long to grow.

Subhadra, meanwhile, knew nothing of the two men who had stopped to look at her, or of the plan already taking shape behind Krishna's easy manner. She stood among her maids at the bright center of the festival, and the day went on around her.
reflection: The comedy sits beside the warmth: the mightiest archer of his age stopped still by a glance, and Krishna too fond of him to leave him stranded there. Friendship here looks like a knowing smile and an offer to manage everything — and a nudge toward a bolder path than waiting.
hero_scene: Arjuna stopped in the middle of the Raivataka festival, gazing at Subhadra decked in ornaments among her maids, while Krishna stands beside him watching with a knowing smile.
